images.caption: Figure 1:Interface comparison.Mobile ALOHA exhibits perception and mobility gaps, while our interface aligns human–robot perception and preserves natural operator mobility.

Figure 2:HALO overview and learned capabilities.(a) Human-aligned data collection with natural locomotion and direct bimanual kinesthetic teaching.
(b) Learned policies exhibit precise manipulation, coordinated whole-body control, long-horizon mobile manipulation, and navigation.

Figure 3:Kinesthetic end-effector redesign.Compared with the ALOHA end-effector, we remove the handle-and-scissor design for kinesthetic teaching. The handle limits access near the table surface, while the scissor mechanism is less convenient for forceful manipulation. Our design increases hand contact area, enabling compact and stable physical control.

Figure 4:HALO deployment system overview.Hardware configuration includes the dual-arm manipulation interface, onboard cameras, differential-drive base, encoders, and computing system. The base is removed during data collection.

Figure 5:Implicit base control.The low-resistance collection platform allows base motion to arise naturally from the operator’s movement, without explicit base control that could disrupt hand manipulation, thereby capturing coordinated mobile manipulation behaviors.
Figure 7:Visual processing.Our pipeline removes human hands during rapid motion, bimanual manipulation, and egocentric interaction.

Figure 8:Comparison and limitations of demonstration data collection.Top:Comparison of human demonstration collection methods in terms of efficiency and reliability.
Succ. Rate and Time denote the demonstration success rate and the average duration of successful demonstrations, respectively.Bottom:Representative limitations of existing teleoperation interfaces: VR lacks precise gripper control and force feedback, while the mobile base constrains operator mobility during whole-body demonstration collection.

Figure 9:Push Chair, Zip-Tie Fastening, and Disassemble Lego.In Push Chair, the policy navigates to the chair, grasps it while moving, transports it to the target desk, and inserts it into place.
Both Zip-Tie Fastening and Disassemble Lego require precise action prediction. In Disassemble Lego, the randomized separation pattern changes the required disassembly strategy. The policy learns to handle these variations from our demonstrations and generalizes to unseen Lego configurations. In the third row, two Lego pieces of the same color are included, and the policy correctly places both resulting pieces into the correct bin.

Figure 10:Long-horizon mobile manipulation with coordinated whole-body control.The policy retrieves a box from the shelf, loads target objects, transports the box to the conveyor, places it at the designated location, and returns to repeat the procedure.

Figure 11:Generalization of mobile manipulation.We evaluatePush Chairunder large initial-pose variations and in unseen environments. Compared with the 5–10 cm initial-position variation in Mobile ALOHA, we increase the randomization to 2–3 m.
